question: Under Georgia's statute of frauds, O.C.G.A. Section 13-5-30(4), what form must a contract for the sale of land generally take to be enforceable?
choice_a: It must be in writing and signed by the party to be charged
choice_b: It may be entirely oral as long as two adult witnesses can later confirm the terms
choice_c: It must be recorded with the county clerk within 10 days of formation to be enforceable at all
choice_d: It must be notarized by a Georgia attorney, even before any dispute arises
explanation: O.C.G.A. Section 13-5-30(4) requires that any contract for the sale of lands, or any interest in or concerning lands, be in writing and signed by the party to be charged (or that party's lawfully authorized agent) to be enforceable.

question: Under O.C.G.A. Section 44-5-30, what execution formalities must a Georgia deed generally satisfy?
choice_a: It need only be signed by the grantor, with no witnesses or officer attestation required under any circumstance
choice_b: It must be in writing, signed, and attested by an officer plus one witness, and delivered for consideration
choice_c: It must be attested by three separate witnesses and two notaries
choice_d: It must be delivered to the county tax assessor before it can be signed by the grantor
explanation: O.C.G.A. Section 44-5-30 sets out Georgia deed execution formalities: the deed must be in writing, signed, attested by an officer (such as a notary) plus one additional witness, and delivered for consideration to be effective.

question: Does Georgia law require a deed to follow a specific prescribed form or set of magic words to be valid?
choice_a: Yes -- Georgia law mandates a single statutory deed form that must be used verbatim in every transaction
choice_b: Yes -- only a deed drafted personally by the Georgia Real Estate Commission is valid
choice_c: No -- O.C.G.A. Section 44-5-33 states that no prescribed form is essential to a deed's validity, provided the document is sufficient in itself to make known the transaction
choice_d: No -- Georgia law has no deed validity requirements of any kind
explanation: O.C.G.A. Section 44-5-33 states that no prescribed form is essential to the validity of a deed, so long as the instrument is sufficient in itself to make known the transaction it accomplishes -- Georgia does not mandate a single mandatory statutory deed template.

question: Under O.C.G.A. Section 44-5-61, does Georgia law imply a warranty of title in an ordinary sale of land unless the parties say otherwise?
choice_a: Yes -- every Georgia land sale automatically carries a full implied warranty of title regardless of the deed's language
choice_b: Yes, but only for sales involving licensed real estate brokers
choice_c: No -- Georgia law prohibits any warranty of title from ever being included in a deed
choice_d: No -- Georgia law states that in a sale of land there is no implied warranty of title, so a warranty of title must be express to exist
explanation: O.C.G.A. Section 44-5-61 provides that in a sale of land there is no implied warranty of title -- meaning a Georgia grantor's warranty of title must be expressly stated in the deed to exist; it is never automatically implied by law.

question: Under O.C.G.A. Section 44-5-62, what does a Georgia general warranty of title covenant typically include?
choice_a: Right-to-sell, quiet enjoyment, and freedom from encumbrances
choice_b: A guarantee of the property's future market appreciation
choice_c: A guarantee that the property is free of all defects discoverable only by a licensed home inspector
choice_d: A guarantee that the buyer will obtain financing on specific terms
explanation: O.C.G.A. Section 44-5-62 sets out that a general warranty of title covenant includes the grantor's right to sell the property, the grantee's quiet enjoyment of the property, and freedom from encumbrances -- these are the substantive protections an express warranty of title provides under Georgia law.

question: A Georgia grantor conveys property using a deed that contains no express language warranting title. Under O.C.G.A. Section 44-5-61, what warranty of title does the grantee receive by default?
choice_a: A full general warranty of title is implied automatically regardless of the deed's silence
choice_b: None -- because Georgia does not imply a warranty of title, the grantee receives whatever protection the deed's express language provides, and none if the deed is silent on the point
choice_c: A limited warranty covering only defects arising during the grantor's ownership, implied automatically
choice_d: The grantee automatically receives title insurance issued by the State of Georgia in place of any warranty
explanation: Because O.C.G.A. Section 44-5-61 provides that there is no implied warranty of title in a Georgia land sale, a deed that is silent on warranty language conveys no warranty of title -- any warranty protection must be expressly stated in the deed itself.

question: What type of security instrument does Georgia use to secure a real estate loan, under O.C.G.A. Section 44-14-60?
choice_a: A classic deed of trust, in which title is held by a neutral third-party trustee on behalf of the lender
choice_b: A simple promissory note with no instrument conveying any interest in the real property at all
choice_c: A security deed, which passes title to the property directly to the grantee (lender) until the debt is fully paid -- a title-theory instrument with no third-party trustee
choice_d: A judicial mortgage lien that requires court approval before it can attach to the property
explanation: O.C.G.A. Section 44-14-60 establishes Georgia's security deed (deed to secure debt): a conveyance that passes title to the property to the grantee (lender) until the debt is fully paid, and which is treated as an absolute conveyance, not a mortgage -- a title-theory instrument that, unlike a classic deed of trust, involves no third-party trustee.

question: How does a Georgia security deed under O.C.G.A. Section 44-14-60 differ from a classic 'deed of trust' used in some other states?
choice_a: There is no meaningful difference; the two instruments are legally identical in every respect
choice_b: A Georgia security deed requires judicial foreclosure, while a deed of trust never does
choice_c: A Georgia security deed can only be used for commercial property, while a deed of trust can only be used for residential property
choice_d: A Georgia security deed conveys title directly to the grantee (lender) with no third-party trustee involved, whereas a classic deed of trust conveys title to a neutral third-party trustee who holds it on the lender's behalf
explanation: The facts sheet emphasizes that Georgia's security deed is legally distinct from a classic deed of trust: it conveys title directly to the grantee/lender under O.C.G.A. Section 44-14-60, with no third-party trustee, even though the two instruments are functionally similar in securing a debt with real property.

question: Under O.C.G.A. Section 44-14-162, is a court order or judicial proceeding required to foreclose under a Georgia security deed's power of sale?
choice_a: No -- Georgia is a nonjudicial power-of-sale foreclosure state; the sale must be advertised and conducted in the usual manner of the sheriff's sales, with the security instrument filed with the superior court clerk before sale, but no court order is required
choice_b: Yes -- Georgia requires a full judicial foreclosure proceeding, including a trial, for every security deed foreclosure
choice_c: Yes, but only if the borrower requests a judicial hearing in writing
choice_d: No court involvement of any kind is required or permitted at any stage of a Georgia foreclosure
explanation: O.C.G.A. Section 44-14-162 provides that a sale under a power in a security deed must be advertised and conducted in the usual manner of the sheriff's sales, with the security instrument filed with the superior court clerk before the sale -- but no court order or judicial proceeding is required, making Georgia a nonjudicial power-of-sale foreclosure state.

question: A borrower defaults on a loan secured by a Georgia security deed containing a power-of-sale clause. What is the general foreclosure process the lender must follow under O.C.G.A. Section 44-14-162?
choice_a: The lender must file a civil lawsuit and obtain a final judgment of foreclosure from a superior court judge before any sale can occur
choice_b: The lender advertises and conducts the sale in the manner of a sheriff's sale, after filing the security instrument with the superior court clerk, without needing to obtain a court order first
choice_c: The lender must obtain the unanimous written consent of all neighboring property owners before advertising the sale
choice_d: The lender automatically takes title without any sale or advertisement process whatsoever
explanation: Because Georgia is a nonjudicial power-of-sale foreclosure state under O.C.G.A. Section 44-14-162, the lender advertises and conducts the sale in the manner of a sheriff's sale after filing the security instrument with the superior court clerk, without first needing to obtain a court order or judgment.

question: What are the essential elements generally required to form a valid, legally binding contract, including a real estate purchase contract?
choice_a: Offer and acceptance only -- consideration is never required for a real estate contract
choice_b: A notarized signature and a filing with the county recorder, with no offer or acceptance required
choice_c: Offer, acceptance, consideration, capacity of the parties, and a legal purpose
choice_d: Verbal agreement plus part performance, with no writing needed under any circumstance
explanation: Under general contract-law doctrine, a valid contract requires a valid offer, acceptance of that offer, consideration exchanged between the parties, legal capacity of the parties to contract, and a lawful purpose.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate contract-law doctrine, not Georgia-statute-specific

question: What is the function of a contingency clause, such as a financing or inspection contingency, in a real estate purchase contract?
choice_a: It permanently voids the contract the moment it is signed by both parties
choice_b: It obligates the seller to pay for all of the buyer's closing costs regardless of the contract's other terms
choice_c: It has no legal effect unless separately notarized by a Georgia attorney
choice_d: It makes a party's performance under the contract conditional on a specified future event occurring, allowing that party to withdraw without breach if the condition is not satisfied
explanation: A contingency clause conditions a party's obligation to perform on a specified future event (such as obtaining financing or a satisfactory inspection); if the condition fails, the contingent party may typically withdraw from the contract without being considered in breach.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate contract-law doctrine, not Georgia-statute-specific

question: What is the difference between a void contract, a voidable contract, and an unenforceable contract?
choice_a: A void contract has no legal effect from the outset; a voidable contract is valid until a party with the legal right to do so elects to disaffirm it; an unenforceable contract may otherwise be valid but cannot be enforced in court, often due to a defense such as the statute of frauds
choice_b: The three terms all describe exactly the same legal outcome and are used interchangeably
choice_c: A void contract can always be ratified later by either party, while a voidable contract can never be ratified
choice_d: An unenforceable contract is always also void from its inception
explanation: A void contract never had legal effect, a voidable contract remains valid and enforceable unless and until a party with the power to do so elects to disaffirm it (such as a minor), and an unenforceable contract may be otherwise valid in substance but cannot be enforced in court due to a legal defense, such as failing to satisfy a statute of frauds writing requirement.
source_note: hedge: standard national contract-law doctrine, not Georgia-statute-specific

question: What is an option agreement in the context of real estate contracts?
choice_a: A contract that obligates both parties to close the transaction regardless of market conditions
choice_b: A contract in which, for consideration, an optionor grants an optionee the exclusive right, but not the obligation, to purchase (or lease) a property on specified terms within a stated period
choice_c: A type of deed used exclusively to convey mineral rights
choice_d: A contract that automatically becomes a lease once signed, with no purchase component possible
explanation: An option agreement gives the optionee (holder of the option) the exclusive right -- but not an obligation -- to purchase or lease property on agreed terms within a specified time period, in exchange for consideration paid to the optionor; the optionee may simply let the option lapse if they choose not to exercise it.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate contract-law doctrine, not Georgia-statute-specific

question: What remedies are generally available to a non-breaching party when the other party breaches a real estate purchase contract?
choice_a: No remedies are available for breach of a real estate contract under any circumstance
choice_b: The only available remedy for any breach is automatic criminal prosecution of the breaching party
choice_c: Remedies such as rescission, compensatory damages, or specific performance, depending on the circumstances and the contract's own terms
choice_d: The non-breaching party's only option is to forfeit their own earnest money regardless of who breached
explanation: General contract-law remedies for breach of a real estate purchase contract can include rescission (unwinding the contract), compensatory (monetary) damages, or specific performance (a court order compelling the breaching party to complete the transaction), with the appropriate remedy depending on the facts and the contract's own terms, such as a liquidated damages clause.
source_note: hedge: standard national contract-law doctrine, not Georgia-statute-specific

question: What is the general mechanic behind a deed that conveys 'whatever interest, if any, the grantor actually holds' in a property, with no warranty of title made by the grantor?
choice_a: This describes a general warranty deed, which always includes the broadest possible warranty of title
choice_b: This type of conveyance is not legally possible under any circumstances and would automatically be void
choice_c: This describes a security deed, which conveys title to a lender to secure a debt
choice_d: This describes the general, standard-industry mechanics of a quitclaim-type conveyance -- it transfers only the grantor's existing interest, without any title warranty, and is commonly used to clear a cloud on title or convey an interest between related parties
explanation: As a matter of general/standard conveyancing mechanics, a deed that conveys only whatever interest the grantor actually has, without any warranty of title, functions as a quitclaim-type conveyance -- commonly used to clear title clouds or convey interests between related parties. This is treated as general/standard content because Georgia's own deed statutes do not use or define the term 'quitclaim deed' by that specific name.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate conveyancing mechanics; Georgia deed statutes (O.C.G.A. Section 44-5-33) do not use the specific term 'quitclaim deed,' so no Georgia-specific citation is asserted for this term

question: A Georgia broker's client asks whether an oral agreement to sell a vacant lot, confirmed only by a handshake, is legally enforceable against the seller. What should the broker explain, based on Georgia's statute of frauds?
choice_a: The agreement is generally not enforceable, because O.C.G.A. Section 13-5-30(4) requires a contract for the sale of land to be in writing and signed by the party to be charged
choice_b: The agreement is fully enforceable because Georgia has no writing requirement for land sale contracts
choice_c: The agreement is enforceable only if the purchase price is under a specific statutory dollar threshold
choice_d: The agreement is enforceable as long as a licensed real estate agent personally witnessed the handshake
explanation: Because O.C.G.A. Section 13-5-30(4) requires a land sale contract to be in writing and signed by the party to be charged, a purely oral agreement -- even one confirmed by a handshake -- is generally unenforceable in Georgia.
